question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer:
When thin fuel is ignited in the middle at low forced-flow speeds in microgravity, the flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow, unlike in normal gravity where it spreads downstream [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Results from space station tests indicate that materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. During microgravity experiments on fabrics such as Nomex and a 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass blend, airflow was directed along the fuel surface in opposed or concurrent directions at speeds reaching up to 40 cm/s [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Researchers hypothesize that with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity burn as well as or better than in normal gravity [PSI-25 · doi:10.60555/4qc4-de67]. 

Our sources do not cover specific numerical flame spread rates across different fabric types.

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Four NASA PSI experiments tested oxygen levels above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]. 

Specifically:
- PSI-159 ACME CFI-G tested oxygen concentrations from 12% to 85% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64].
- PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design tested oxygen concentrations from 19.8048% to 84.9978% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45].
- PSI-20 ACME BRE tested oxygen concentrations from 21% to 40% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72].
- PSI-69 FLEX tested oxygen concentrations from 12% to 34% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

Our sources do not cover whether oxygen levels above 30% were tested in PSI-21, PSI-22, PSI-26, PSI-47, PSI-60, PSI-62, PSI-100, PSI-101, PSI-102, PSI-106, PSI-107, PSI-115, PSI-117, or PSI-142, as oxygen data was not reported for these experiments [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
Smoke detection on the ISS was tested through experiments like the Dust Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), which measured background aerosol levels, and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), which examined smoke particle-size distributions from spacecraft materials [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. In SAME testing, solid fuels including Teflon, Kapton, Silicone Rubber, Lampwick, and Dibutyl Phthalate were tested in microgravity with airflows of 5–10 cm/s across 4 experimental test rows using smoke detectors, video cameras, and soot samplers [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62].

This testing matters because microgravity produces vastly different smoke particle sizes than Earth gravity, which can alter detector responses and prevent alarms from triggering [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. The experiments provide baseline reduced-gravity data to design reliable fire detection systems for future long-duration space missions [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202]. Additionally, these advances help create better smoke detectors to save lives in extreme Earth environments like submarines and underwater laboratories [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer:
In a drop tower test on a PMMA sphere, nitrogen gas was applied to extinguish the flame [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Nitrogen was also applied to selected flames in microgravity testing, though early results showed it could actually strengthen a flame depending on entrainment [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Other gases—such as carbon dioxide (CO2), helium (He), xenon, and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6)—are identified as planned or target suppressants to be evaluated in the FLEX experiment [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. Additionally, the BASS experiment aims to assess an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. 

Our sources do not cover specific test results detailing which of the other planned suppressant gases successfully extinguished flames in completed experiments [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451][PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80][PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On February 24, 1997, a fire ignited in a solid fuel oxygen generator inside the Kvant-1 module aboard the space station Mir [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, blocked access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles, and filled the modules with toxic smoke [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The six crew members extinguished the fire in narrow confines with no structural damage to the station or lasting harm to themselves, and life support cleared the smoke over several hours [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. 

Lessons from the incident were incorporated into the design and operations of the International Space Station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Russian space officials updated crew emergency training, ground controller responses, and ground preparation for solid fuel oxygen generator canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Furthermore, the International Space Station implemented redundant oxygen generation systems with improved safety measures [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon gravity?
answer:
The NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository contains no real partial-gravity combustion data and zero investigations conducted in real Moon gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. The closest PSI investigation is PSI-22, which used an electric field to mimic partial gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. 

Ground-based simulated lunar gravity testing has been conducted, such as drop tower centrifuge tests observing fabric burning in simulated lunar gravity [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. Real lunar surface combustion data is planned for the future through the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment, which is to be performed on the Moon at its 1/6 reduced gravity level [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are a low-temperature combustion regime that form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures between 500 and 1000 K [PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. They can form after visible flame extinction and continue to burn for a prolonged period [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science].

Cool flames present a fire risk because reduced-gravity environments are particularly conducive to this low-temperature combustion regime, impacting spacecraft fire safety [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Furthermore, cool flames burn only a fraction of the fuel vaporized from a droplet surface, which leaves behind a fuel vapor cloud when the cool flame extinguishes [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Research into these microgravity combustion dynamics aims to refine knowledge to support the design of safer spacecraft systems [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].
